the distribution of health planning responsibilities between the central and peripheral levels in the four countries of Trinidad and Tobago; the Bahamas; Martinique and Suriname.
the distribution of health planning functions and the management of health services between the centre and periphery.

there is a trend towards decentralised planning, with greater hospital autonomy and regionalisation.
decentralisation is an issue of continuing importance, but that there are no clear-cut solutions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the decentralisation of planning and management functions in the health sector is a desirable objective, the process of achieving this goal has been complex, slow, and difficult.

the historical distribution of health planning responsibilities has been a function of colonial history, and that recent reform trends are a response to the problems of the centralised systems that have been inherited.

the decentralisation reforms in the Caribbean have been driven by the need to improve the efficiency of the health system and by the availability of external funding, and have involved the creation of agencies to which the central government has delegated authority, and in some cases the creation of regional health authorities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the historical patterns of decentralisation in the four territories were strongly influenced by their different colonial backgrounds, and that the recent reforms were strongly influenced by the political and economic circumstances of the time.
the historical and political contexts of decentralisation are crucial in understanding why reforms are introduced and how they are implemented.
the decentralisation reforms in these territories were not driven by a single, overarching theory of decentralisation, but were rather pragmatic responses to a range of problems and opportunities.
